title: Trigonometry
lines: USAT trigonometry questions check standard values, signs in the four quadrants, identities, compound and double angles, periods, solutions of simple equations, and the principal values of inverse functions. Fast recall of the standard table and the main identities is the key; most answers need two lines.
## Angles and standard values
- π radians = 180°, so 1 rad ≈ 57.3°. Arc length l = rθ and sector area = ½r²θ, with θ in radians.
| θ | sin θ | cos θ | tan θ
| 90° (π/2) | 1 | 0 | undefined
- Memory aid: sin 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90° = √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2; cos runs the list backwards.
## Signs and identities
- "All Students Take Coffee": in quadrant I all ratios are positive, in II sin (and cosec), in III tan (and cot), in IV cos (and sec).
- Pythagorean identities: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ, 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.
- Negative angles: sin(−θ) = −sin θ, cos(−θ) = cos θ, tan(−θ) = −tan θ.
- Allied angles: 90° ± θ and 270° ± θ change sin to cos and tan to cot; 180° ± θ and 360° − θ keep the same ratio. The sign comes from the quadrant.
## Compound and double angles
- sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B.
- cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B (the sign flips).
- tan(A ± B) = (tan A ± tan B)/(1 ∓ tan A tan B).
> Example 1. Find sin 75° exactly.
- sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A; cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A; tan 2A = 2 tan A/(1 − tan²A).
> Example 2. sin A = 3/5 and A lies in quadrant II. Find cos A, tan A and sin 2A.
> cos A = −√(1 − 9/25) = −4/5 (cos is negative in quadrant II). tan A = −3/4. sin 2A = 2 × 3/5 × (−4/5) = −24/25.
- Half angles: sin²(A/2) = (1 − cos A)/2 and cos²(A/2) = (1 + cos A)/2.
- Triple angles: sin 3A = 3 sin A − 4 sin³A and cos 3A = 4 cos³A − 3 cos A.
- Sum to product: sin C + sin D = 2 sin((C + D)/2) cos((C − D)/2); cos C + cos D = 2 cos((C + D)/2) cos((C − D)/2).
## Graphs and periods
| Function | Range | Period
| sin x, cos x | −1 to 1 | 2π
| tan x, cot x | all real numbers | π
| sec x, cosec x | ≤ −1 or ≥ 1 | 2π
- sin(ax + b) and cos(ax + b) have period 2π/|a|; tan(ax + b) has period π/|a|.
- a sin x + b cos x lies between −√(a² + b²) and +√(a² + b²); for example, 3 sin x + 4 cos x has a maximum of 5.
## Laws for any triangle
- Sine rule: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C = 2R, where R is the circumradius.
- Cosine rule: a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A.
- Area = ½bc sin A, or Hero's formula √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)) with s = (a + b + c)/2.
## Trigonometric equations
- First find the principal solution, then all the angles in the required interval using the quadrant signs.
- General solutions (n any integer): sin θ = 0 gives θ = nπ; cos θ = 0 gives θ = (2n + 1)π/2; tan θ = k gives θ = α + nπ; cos θ = k gives θ = 2nπ ± α; sin θ = k gives θ = nπ + (−1)ⁿα.
- Quadratic equations in sin θ or cos θ: factorise, then reject any value outside −1 to 1.
> Example 3. Solve 2cos²θ − 3cos θ + 1 = 0 for 0 ≤ θ < 2π.
> (2cos θ − 1)(cos θ − 1) = 0, so cos θ = ½ or 1. cos θ = ½ gives π/3 and 5π/3; cos θ = 1 gives 0. The solutions are 0, π/3 and 5π/3.
## Inverse trigonometric functions
| Function | Domain | Principal values
| sin⁻¹x | −1 ≤ x ≤ 1 | −π/2 to π/2
| cos⁻¹x | −1 ≤ x ≤ 1 | 0 to π
| tan⁻¹x | all real x | between −π/2 and π/2
- sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2 and tan⁻¹x + cot⁻¹x = π/2.
- tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹y = tan⁻¹((x + y)/(1 − xy)) when xy < 1.
- cos⁻¹(−x) = π − cos⁻¹x, but sin⁻¹(−x) = −sin⁻¹x.
> Example 4. Evaluate tan⁻¹(1/2) + tan⁻¹(1/3).
! sin⁻¹(sin θ) = θ only when θ lies between −π/2 and π/2. So sin⁻¹(sin 5π/6) = π/6.
! Never divide both sides of an equation by sin θ or cos θ: you lose the solutions where it is zero. Factorise instead.
! Use radians in l = rθ and in calculus; degrees give wrong answers.
## Quick check
- Value of cos 60° + sin 30°? (1)
- Period of sin 3x? (2π/3)
- Sign of tan 200°? (positive, quadrant III)
- Simplify 1 − 2sin²15°. (cos 30° = √3/2)
- Principal value of cos⁻¹(−½)? (2π/3)
